text: Yasser Arafat (c. August 1929 – 11 November 2004), also known by his kunya Abu Ammar, was a Palestinian political leader who served as chairman of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) from 1969 to 2004, President of Palestine from 1989 to 2004, and President of the Palestinian Authority (PNA) from 1994 to 2004. Ideologically an Arab nationalist and socialist, he was a founding member of the Fatah political party, which he led from 1959 until 2004. Born in Cairo, Egypt, to Palestinian parents, Arafat spent most of his youth there and studied at the University of King Fuad I, graduating in 1950 with a degree in civil engineering. While a student, he embraced Arab nationalist and anti-Zionist ideas and engaged in discussions with Jews, reading works by Theodor Herzl and other Zionists. In 1946, he began procuring weapons for Palestinian irregulars. During the 1948 Arab–Israeli War, he fought alongside the Muslim Brotherhood in the Gaza area, though he did not join the organization. After the war, he returned to Cairo and served as president of the General Union of Palestinian Students from 1952 to 1956. In the late 1950s, he co-founded Fatah, a paramilitary organization that sought to replace Israel with a Palestinian state, which operated from several Arab countries and launched attacks on Israeli targets. In 1967, he joined the PLO and was elected chair of the Palestinian National Council (PNC) in 1969. Fatah's growing presence in Jordan led to military clashes with King Hussein’s government, prompting its relocation to Lebanon, where it assisted the Lebanese National Movement during the Lebanese Civil War and continued attacks on Israel, becoming a major target of Israeli invasions during the 1978 South Lebanon conflict and the 1982 Lebanon War. From 1983 to 1993, Arafat based himself in Tunisia and shifted toward negotiation. In 1988, he acknowledged Israel's right to exist and advocated a two-state solution. In 1994, he returned to Palestine, settling in Gaza City, and promoted self-governance for Palestinian territories. He engaged in negotiations with Israel, including the Madrid Conference of 1991, the 1993 Oslo Accords, and the 2000 Camp David Summit. The Oslo Accords led to Arafat being awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1994 alongside Israeli prime ministers Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres. His support among Palestinians declined due to the rise of Hamas and other militant groups. In late 2004, after being confined in his Ramallah compound by the Israeli army for over two years, Arafat fell into a coma and died; the cause of death remains speculative, with investigations by Russian, French, and Swiss teams concluding no foul play was involved, though a Swiss team found radiological poisoning. Arafat remains a controversial figure: Palestinians view him as a martyr symbolizing national aspirations, while many Israelis regard him as a terrorist. Palestinian rivals, including Islamists and PLO radicals, criticized him as corrupt or too accommodating to Israel. Arafat's full name was Mohammed Abdel Rahman Abdel Raouf Arafat al-Qudwa al-Husseini. He dropped most of his inherited names, adopting Yasser in the early 1950s and the nom de guerre Abu Ammar during his guerrilla career, both linked to Ammar ibn Yasir, a companion of Muhammad. He was raised in Cairo, where the tradition of dropping the first name was common, and retained "Arafat" due to its Islamic significance. In 1956, after the Suez Crisis, he was expelled from Sinai and Gaza by the UN Emergency Force. He attempted to obtain visas to Canada and Saudi Arabia, which were denied, and later secured a visa to Kuwait in 1957, where he met Salah Khalaf ("Abu Iyad") and Khalil al-Wazir ("Abu Jihad"), both of whom became his top aides. In 1962, Arafat and his associates moved to Syria, where Fatah had about three hundred members, none of whom were fighters. He recruited members by offering higher salaries than those in the Palestine Liberation Army (PLO), and in December 1967, a Fatah squad attempted to infiltrate Israel and was intercepted. Arafat was detained in Syria’s Mezzeh Prison after the killing of Palestinian Syrian Army officer Yusef Urabi, who was killed during a meeting between Arafat and Ahmed Jibril; Arafat was sentenced to death but pardoned by President Salah Jadid. On 13 November 1966, Israel launched a raid on as-Samu in the West Bank in response to a roadside bomb attack that killed three Israeli security personnel, resulting in the deaths of many Jordanian forces and the destruction of 125 homes, a key factor leading to the 1967 Six-Day War. The war began on 5 June 1967 with Israeli air strikes on Egypt’s air force and ended with an Arab defeat and Israeli occupation of the West Bank and Gaza Strip. Despite the defeat, Arafat and Fatah gained influence as Palestinians began to see a Palestinian-led solution as essential, leading to the collapse of other Palestinian parties aligned with Arab governments. After the defeat, Arafat crossed the Jordan River and established recruitment centers in Hebron, Jerusalem, and Nablus. Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser declared Arafat the "leader of the Palestinians." In December 1967, Ahmad Shukeiri resigned as PLO chairman, and Yahya Hammuda appointed Arafat, allocating Fatah 33 of 105 seats in the PLO Executive Committee. Throughout 1968, Fatah and other Palestinian groups were targeted in the Israeli military operation at Karameh, a Jordanian village housing a major PLO camp. The operation, in response to attacks on Israeli civilians, including a school bus bombing in the Negev that killed two children, aimed to destroy the camp and capture Arafat. Though advised to withdraw, Arafat refused, stating that he wanted to demonstrate that some in the Arab world would not flee, and the Jordanian Army agreed to support Fatah if heavy fighting occurred. The operation was planned in 1967, one year before the school bus attack. The size of the Israeli forces entering Karameh led the Jordanians to believe Israel intended to occupy the eastern bank of the Jordan River.

The Front for the Liberation of Palestine (DFLP) was ordered to withdraw their forces from the town of Karameh, Jordan, but Arafat refused, stating, "We want to convince the world that there are those in the Arab world who will not withdraw or flee," and insisted that Fatah remain despite advice from a sympathetic Jordanian Army divisional commander to retreat to the hills. Arafat's orders ensured Fatah stayed, with the Jordanian Army agreeing to support them if heavy fighting occurred. In response to persistent PLO raids on Israeli civilian targets, Israel launched an attack on Karameh, aiming to destroy the PLO camp and capture Yasser Arafat in retaliation for attacks that culminated in an Israeli school bus hitting a mine in the Negev, killing two children. Plans for both the PLO raids and the Israeli invasion were prepared in 1967, one year before the bus attack. The size of the Israeli forces entering Karameh led Jordanians to believe Israel intended to occupy the eastern bank of the Jordan River, including the Balqa Governorate, to create a situation similar to the Golan Heights, captured just 10 months earlier. Israel assumed the Jordanian Army would ignore the invasion, but instead fought alongside the Palestinians, opening heavy fire that inflicted losses on Israeli forces. This engagement marked the first known use of suicide bombers by Palestinian forces. The Israelis were repelled at the end of a day's battle, destroying most of the Karameh camp and capturing around 141 PLO prisoners. Both sides declared victory; on a tactical level, Israel won, and the camp was destroyed, though the relatively high casualties were a surprise to the Israel Defense Forces and shocking to Israelis. King Hussein allowed the Palestinians to take credit for the victory. Although Arafat's direct presence on the battlefield is unclear, his allies and Israeli intelligence confirm he urged his men to hold their ground and continue fighting. The battle was widely covered by Time, and Arafat's face appeared on the cover of the 13 December 1968 issue, bringing his image to the world for the first time. This turning point elevated Arafat and Fatah's profiles, making him a national hero who dared to confront Israel. Mass applause from the Arab world led to significant financial donations, improved weaponry and equipment, and a surge in Fatah's membership, including thousands of non-Palestinians. At the Palestinian National Council (PNC) meeting in Cairo on 3 February 1969, Yahya Hammuda stepped down as PLO chairman, and Arafat was elected chairman on 4 February. He became Commander-in-Chief of the Palestinian Revolutionary Forces two years later and head of the PLO's political department in 1973. In the late 1960s, tensions between Palestinians and the Jordanian government intensified as heavily armed Palestinian elements created a virtual "state within a state," controlling strategic positions in Jordan. After their victory in Karameh, Fatah and other Palestinian militias began taking control of civil life, setting up roadblocks, humiliating Jordanian police, molesting women, and levying illegal taxes—actions Arafat either condoned or ignored. King Hussein viewed this as a threat to his sovereignty and security and attempted to disarm the militias, dismissing several anti-PLO cabinet officials, including family members, and inviting Arafat to become Deputy Prime Minister of Jordan, which Arafat refused, citing his belief in a Palestinian state with Palestinian leadership. Despite Hussein's intervention, militant actions continued. On 15 September 1970, the PFLP hijacked four planes, landing three at Dawson's Field, 30 miles (48 km) east of Amman; after foreign hostages were removed, three planes were blown up in front of international press, damaging Arafat's image in Western nations, including the United States. Arafat publicly condemned the hijackings and suspended the PFLP from guerrilla actions, taking the same action after the PFLP attacked Athens Airport. The Jordanian government moved to regain control, declaring martial law on the same day, and Arafat became supreme commander of the PLA. Arab governments attempted to negotiate a peaceful resolution, with Gamal Abdel Nasser leading the first emergency Arab League summit in Cairo on 21 September. Arafat's speech won sympathy from Arab leaders, and some, like Muammar Gaddafi, mocked Hussein and his father, King Talal. A ceasefire was agreed upon, but Nasser died of a heart attack hours after the summit, and the conflict resumed. By 25 September, the Jordanian Army achieved dominance, and two days later Arafat and Hussein agreed to a ceasefire in Amman. The Jordanian Army inflicted heavy casualties on Palestinians, including civilians, with approximately 3,500 fatalities. After repeated ceasefire violations, Arafat called for King Hussein to be toppled. In June 1971, Hussein ordered his forces to remove all remaining Palestinian fighters from northern Jordan, which they accomplished. Arafat and several of his forces, including high-ranking commanders Abu Iyad and Abu Jihad, were forced into the northern corner of Jordan and relocated near Jerash, near the Syria border. With the help of Munib Masri, a pro-Palestinian Jordanian cabinet member, and Fahd al-Khomeimi, the Saudi ambassador to Jordan, Arafat managed to enter Syria with nearly two thousand fighters. However, due to hostility between Arafat and Syrian President Hafez al-Assad, who had ousted President Salah Jadid, the fighters crossed into Lebanon to join PLO forces there, establishing a new headquarters. Because of Lebanon's weak central government, the PLO operated virtually as an independent state. During the 1970s, numerous leftist PLO groups carried out attacks against Israeli civilians and military targets. In 1972, the Fatah subgroup Black September hijacked Sabena Flight 572 en route to Vienna, forcing it to land at Ben Gurion International Airport in Israel. The PFLP and the Japanese Red Army carried out a shooting rampage at the same airport, killing twenty-four civilians. Israel claimed the assassination of PFLP spokesman Ghassan Kanafani was a response to the PFLP's role in the attack, and two days later, various PLO factions retaliated by bombing a bus station, killing eleven civilians. At the Munich Olympic Games, Black September kidnapped and killed eleven Israeli athletes. Sources including Mohammed Oudeh (Abu Daoud) and Benny Morris state that Black September was an armed branch of Fatah used for paramilitary operations, and Abu Daoud's 1999 book states Arafat was briefed on plans for the Munich hostage-taking. The killings were internationally condemned. In 1973–74, Arafat closed Black September, ordering the PLO to withdraw from acts of violence outside Israel, the West Bank, and Gaza Strip. In 1974, the PNC approved the Ten Point Program, drawn up by Arafat and his advisers, proposing a Palestinian national authority over all "liberated" Palestinian territory—referring to areas captured in the 1948 Arab–Israeli War (present-day West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Gaza Strip)—causing discontent among factions like the PFLP, DFLP, and others, who formed the Rejectionist Front. Israel and the US have alleged Arafat was involved in the 1973 Khartoum diplomatic assassinations, in which five diplomats and five others were killed. A 1973 U.S. Department of State document, declassified in 2006, concluded "The Khartoum operation was planned and carried out with the full knowledge and personal approval of Yasser Arafat." Arafat denied involvement, claiming it was carried out independently by Black September, and Israel argued he remained in ultimate control, thus not abandoning terrorism. Some U.S. State Department circles viewed Arafat as an able diplomat and negotiator, exemplified by his 1973 effort to arrange a meeting between the President of Iraq and the Emir of Kuwait to resolve their disputes. In 1974, the PLO was declared the "sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people" and admitted to full membership of the Arab League at the Rabat Summit. Arafat became the first representative of a non-governmental organization to address a UN General Assembly plenary session. In his speech, he condemned Zionism but said: "Today I have come bearing an olive branch in one hand and a freedom fighter's rifle in another. Do not let the green branch fall from my hand." He wore a holster throughout the speech, though it did not contain a gun. His speech increased international sympathy for the Palestinian cause. Following recognition, Arafat established relationships with world leaders, including Saddam Hussein and Idi Amin, and was Amin's best man at his wedding in Uganda in 1975. Although hesitant initially, Arafat and Fatah played a significant role in the Lebanese Civil War. Under pressure from PLO sub-groups like the PFLP, DFLP, and the Palestinian Liberation Front (PLF), Arafat aligned the PLO with the Communist and Nasserist Lebanese National Movement (LNM), led by Kamal Jumblatt, who had a friendly relationship with Arafat. Syrian President Hafez al-Assad, fearing a loss of influence, switched sides and sent his army along with Syrian-backed Palestinian factions—As-Sa'iqa and the PFLP-GC led by Ahmad Jibril—to fight alongside Christian forces against the PLO and LNM. The Christian front included the Phalangists loyal to Bachir Gemayel and the Tigers Militia led by Dany Chamoun, son of former President Camille Chamoun. In February 1975, pro-Palestinian Lebanese MP Maarouf Saad was shot and killed, reportedly by the Lebanese Army. His death from wounds the following month, and the April massacre of 27 Palestinians and Lebanese traveling from Sabra and Shatila to Tel al-Zaatar refugee camp by Phalangist forces, triggered the Lebanese Civil War. Arafat was reluctant to respond with force, but many Fatah and PLO members felt otherwise. For example, the DFLP carried out several attacks against the Lebanese Army. In 1976, a Christian militia alliance with Lebanese and Syrian backing besieged Tel al-Zaatar camp in east Beirut. The PLO and LNM retaliated by attacking Damour, a Phalangist stronghold, where they massacred 684 people and wounded many more. The Tel al-Zaatar camp fell to Christians after a six-month siege, during which thousands of Palestinians, mostly civilians, were killed. Arafat and Abu Jihad blamed themselves for failing to organize a rescue effort. PLO cross-border raids against Israel intensified in the late 1970s. One of the most severe, the Coastal Road massacre, occurred on 11 March 1978, when a force of nearly a dozen Fatah fighters landed near a coastal road connecting Haifa and Tel Aviv-Yafo, hijacked a bus, and sprayed gunfire, killing thirty-seven civilians. In response, the IDF launched Operation Litani three days later, achieving control of southern Lebanon up to the Litani River, and Arafat withdrew PLO forces north into Beirut. After Israel withdrew from Lebanon, hostilities continued, though from August 1981 to May 1982, the PLO adopted a policy of refraining from responding to provocations. On 6 June 1982, Israel launched an invasion of Lebanon to expel the PLO from southern Lebanon. Beirut was soon besieged and bombarded by the IDF; Arafat declared the city the "Hanoi and Stalingrad of the Israeli army." The first phase of the war ended, and Arafat, commanding Fatah forces at Tel al-Zaatar, narrowly escaped with help from Saudi and Kuwaiti diplomats. Toward the end of the siege, the U.S. and European governments brokered an agreement guaranteeing safe passage for Arafat and the PLO—guarded by a multinational force of eight hundred U.S. Marines supported by the U.S. Navy—to exile in Tunis. During the war, Arafat took measures to protect the Lebanese Jewish community, ordering PLO fighters to guard the Maghen Abraham Synagogue in Beirut and deliver food to affected families. After Arafat left Lebanon, the synagogue's protection passed to Phalangists. Arafat returned to Lebanon a year after his eviction from Beirut, establishing himself in the northern city of Tripoli. He was expelled by a fellow Palestinian working under Hafez al-Assad and did not return to Lebanon after that second expulsion, though many Fatah fighters did. Arafat and Fatah's operational center was based in Tunis until 1993. In 1985, Arafat narrowly survived an Israeli assassination attempt when Israeli Air Force F-15s bombed his Tunis headquarters as part of Operation Wooden Leg, leaving 73 people dead; Arafat had gone out jogging that morning. The following year, Arafat had his operational headquarters in Baghdad for some time. During the 1980s, Arafat received financial assistance from Libya, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia, enabling him to reconstruct the damaged PLO. This support was especially vital during the First Intifada in December 1987, which began as an uprising of Palestinians against the Israeli occupation of the West Bank and Gaza Strip. The term Intifada, meaning "tremor" in Arabic, is generally defined as an uprising or revolt. The first stage began after an incident at the Erez checkpoint where four Palestinian residents of the Jabalya refugee camp were killed in a traffic accident involving an Israeli driver. Rumors spread that the deaths were a deliberate act of revenge for an Israeli shopper stabbed by a Palestinian in Gaza four days earlier. Mass rioting erupted, and within weeks, following consistent requests by Abu Jihad, Arafat attempted to direct the uprising, which lasted until 1992–93. Abu Jihad, previously assigned responsibility for Palestinian territories within the PLO command, had "impressive knowledge of local conditions" according to biographer Said Aburish and was considered a counterweight to local Palestinian leadership. On 16 April 1988, as the Intifada raged, Abu Jihad was assassinated in his Tunis household by an Israeli hit squad. Arafat had viewed him as a counterweight and led a funeral procession for him in Damascus. The most common tactics used during the Intifada were throwing stones, molotov cocktails, and burning tires. Local leadership in some West Bank towns initiated non-violent protests, including tax resistance and boycotts, and Israel responded by confiscating large sums of money through house-to-house raids. As the Intifada ended, new armed Palestinian groups—particularly Hamas and the Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ)—began targeting Israeli civilians with suicide bombings, and internal Palestinian fighting intensified. In August 1970, Arafat declared: "Our basic aim is to liberate the land from the Mediterranean Sea to the Jordan River. We are not concerned with what took place in June 1967 or in eliminating the consequences of the June war. The Palestinian revolution's basic concern is the uprooting of the Zionist entity from"

During the Intifada, Palestinians commonly used stones, molotov cocktails, and burning tires as their primary tactics, while local West Bank leadership initiated non-violent protests such as tax resistance and boycotts; Israel responded by conducting house-to-house raids and confiscating large sums of money. As the Intifada ended, armed Palestinian groups like Hamas and the Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ) began targeting Israeli civilians with suicide bombings, and internal Palestinian conflict intensified. In August 1970, Arafat declared that the Palestinian goal was to liberate land from the Mediterranean Sea to the Jordan River, rejecting concerns about the 1967 war or Israel's right to exist, though in early 1976 he suggested that if Israel withdrew a "few kilometers" from parts of the West Bank and Gaza Strip and transferred responsibility to the UN, he could acknowledge Israel's right to exist. On 15 November 1988, the PLO proclaimed the independent State of Palestine; despite frequent accusations of terrorism, Arafat repudiated terrorism in all forms, including state terrorism, accepted UN Security Council Resolution 242, and recognized Israel's right to exist in peace and security—statements welcomed by the U.S. administration, signaling a shift from the PLO's original aim of destroying Israel to establishing two separate states: an Israeli state within the 1949 armistice lines and an Arab state in the West Bank and Gaza Strip. On 2 April 1989, Arafat was elected president of the proclaimed State of Palestine by the Central Council of the Palestine National Council. Prior to the 1990–91 Gulf War, Arafat supported Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait and opposed the U.S.-led coalition attack on Iraq without consulting other PLO or Fatah leaders; his top aide, Abu Iyad, opposed the alliance and was assassinated by the Abu Nidal Organization on 17 January 1991. Arafat's decision severed relations with Egypt and many oil-producing Arab states that supported the coalition, and after the war, these states cut off financial support to the PLO and instead funded Hamas and other Islamist groups. On 7 April 1992, Arafat narrowly escaped death when an Air Bissau aircraft he was on crash-landed in the Libyan Desert during a sandstorm, killing two pilots and an engineer and leaving him bruised and shaken. In the early 1990s, Arafat and Fatah officials engaged in secret talks with Israel that led to the 1993 Oslo Accords, which called for Palestinian self-rule in parts of the West Bank and Gaza Strip over five years, a halt to and gradual removal of Israeli settlements, the formation of a Palestinian police force from local recruits and Palestinians abroad, and the transfer of authority over education, culture, social welfare, direct taxation, and tourism to the Palestinian interim government, along with a joint committee for economic cooperation in utilities, industry, trade, and communication. Before signing the accords, Arafat, as PLO Chairman, signed two letters renouncing violence and recognizing Israel, in return for Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin's official recognition of the PLO; the following year, Arafat, Rabin, and Shimon Peres were awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. Palestinian reactions were mixed, with the Rejectionist Front and Islamists opposing the agreements, and Palestinian refugees in Lebanon, Syria, Jordan, and many intellectuals rejecting them, though inhabitants of the territories generally accepted the agreements and Arafat's promises of peace and economic well-being. Under the Oslo terms, Arafat was required to implement PLO authority in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, insisting that financial support was essential to gain acceptance among Palestinians. However, Gulf Arab states, Arafat's usual financial backers, refused to provide major donations due to his support of Iraq in the 1991 Gulf War. Key Fatah negotiator Ahmed Qurei publicly declared the PLO bankrupt. In 1994, Arafat moved to Gaza City, which was under Palestinian National Authority (PNA) control, becoming President and Prime Minister of the PNA, Commander of the PLA, and Speaker of the PLC. In July, the Basic Laws of the PNA were published in three versions by the PLO. Arafat established an executive committee of twenty members, replaced and assigned mayors and city councils in major cities like Gaza and Nablus, subordinated non-governmental organizations in education, health, and social affairs by replacing their leaders with PNA officials loyal to him, and appointed himself chairman of the Palestinian financial organization created by the World Bank to control most aid money. In 1995, Arafat appointed Moshe Hirsch as Minister of Jewish Affairs and established the Preventive Security Service (PSS), active from 13 May 1994, composed mainly of PLA soldiers and foreign Palestinian volunteers, with Mohammed Dahlan and Jibril Rajoub heading it. Amnesty International accused Arafat and the PNA leadership of failing to investigate abuses by the PSS, including torture and unlawful killings, and arrests of human rights activists. From November to December 1995, Arafat toured evacuated Palestinian cities such as Jenin, Ramallah, al-Bireh, Nablus, Qalqilyah, and Tulkarm, declaring them "liberated," and the PNA gained control of the West Bank's postal service. On 20 January 1996, Arafat was elected president of the PNA with 88.2 percent of the vote (the other candidate was Samiha Khalil), though Hamas, the DFLP, and other opposition groups boycotted the election, limiting choices and ensuring Fatah held 51 of the 88 PLC seats. After his election, Arafat was commonly referred to as the Ra'is (president in Arabic), though he referred to himself as "the general." In 1997, the PLC accused the PNA executive branch of financial mismanagement, leading to the resignation of four cabinet members, but Arafat refused to resign. In mid-1996, Benjamin Netanyahu became Israel's Prime Minister, and relations between Palestinian and Israeli leaders deteriorated due to ongoing conflict; despite the Oslo accord, Netanyahu opposed Palestinian statehood. In 1998, President Bill Clinton persuaded the two leaders to meet, resulting in the Wye River Memorandum outlining steps for completing the peace process. In July 2000, Arafat continued negotiations with Ehud Barak at the Camp David Summit, where Barak offered a Palestinian state in 73 percent of the West Bank and all of Gaza, with 90 percent sovereignty over a ten- to twenty-five-year period, including return of a small number of refugees, compensation for those not returning, "custodianship" over Al-Aqsa, sovereignty over all Islamic and Christian holy sites, and three of Jerusalem's four Old City quarters. Arafat rejected the offer and stated, "the Arab leader who would surrender Jerusalem is not born yet." After the September 2000 outbreak of the Second Intifada, talks continued at the Taba Summit in January 2001, but Barak withdrew to campaign; in October and December 2001, suicide bombings by Palestinian militant groups increased and Israeli counter-strikes intensified. Following Ariel Sharon's election in February 2001, the peace process collapsed. Palestinian elections scheduled for January 2002 were postponed due to emergency conditions, IDF incursions, and movement restrictions; on the same day, Sharon ordered Arafat confined to his Mukata'a headquarters in Ramallah after an attack in Hadera, a move supported by U.S. President George W. Bush, who called Arafat "an obstacle to the peace." Arafat's long survival was seen by Western commentators as evidence of his mastery of asymmetric warfare and tactical skill, with some believing his survival was due to Israel's fear that his assassination or arrest would make him a martyr for the Palestinian cause, and others that Israel avoided action because it feared Hamas and other Islamist movements gaining support over Fatah. Israel attempted to assassinate Arafat multiple times but never used its own agents, instead using Palestinian allies through blackmail; according to Alan Hart, Mossad's specialty is poison. In 1970, Abu Iyad reported two attempts by the Mossad and Military Directorate on Arafat's life. In 1976, Palestinian agent Abu Sa'ed was ordered to place poison pellets in Arafat's food, but confessed he could not carry it out because he was a Palestinian and his conscience would not allow it. Arafat claimed in a 1988 Time interview that due to fear of assassination, he never slept in the same place two nights in a row. The rise of Hamas and PIJ, which bombed civilian targets like malls and movie theaters to increase psychological damage, tested Arafat's ability to maintain a unified nationalist movement. In March 2002, a Hamas attack killed 29 Israeli civilians celebrating Passover, including many senior citizens. In response, Israel launched Operation Defensive Shield, a major military offensive into West Bank cities. Mahmoud al-Zahar, a Hamas leader in Gaza, stated in September 2010 that Arafat had instructed Hamas to launch "military operations" against Israel in 2000 when he believed negotiations would fail. Some Israeli officials in 2002 believed al-Aqsa Martyrs' Brigades began attacks to compete with Hamas. On 6 May 2002, Israel released a report, based on documents allegedly seized during a raid on Arafat's Ramallah headquarters, claiming Arafat authorized funding for al-Aqsa Martyrs' Brigades' activities and implicated him in the "planning and execution of terror attacks." Despite persistent Israeli efforts to identify another Palestinian leader, Marwan Barghouti emerged as a possible successor during the Second Intifada but was arrested for allegedly killing 26 civilians and sentenced to five life terms. Arafat was finally allowed to leave his compound on 2 May 2002 after negotiations that resulted in six PFLP militants, including secretary-general Ahmad Sa'adat, being transferred to international custody in Jericho; after the transfer, the siege ended and Arafat issued a call to halt attacks on Israelis on 8 May. On 19 September 2002, the IDF largely demolished the compound with armored bulldozers to isolate Arafat. In March 2003, Arafat ceded his position as Prime Minister to Mahmoud Abbas under U.S. pressure. On 11 September 2003, the Israeli security cabinet decided that "Israel will act to remove this obstacle [Arafat] in the manner, at the time, and in the ways that will be decided on separately." Israeli cabinet members and officials hinted at Arafat's death, military preparations for his expulsion began, and many feared for his life. Israeli peace activists from Gush Shalom, Knesset members, and others entered the compound to serve as a human shield. The compound remained under siege until Arafat was transferred to a French hospital shortly before his death. In 2004, President Bush dismissed Arafat as a negotiating partner, saying he had "failed as a leader" and accused him of undermining Abbas when he was prime minister (Abbas resigned the same year). Arafat had a mixed relationship with Arab leaders, with support increasing when pressured by Israel—for example, when Israel announced in 2003 its intention to remove him from the West Bank. In an interview with Al Jazeera, Arafat responded to Ariel Sharon's suggestion of permanent exile by stating, "Is it his [Sharon's] homeland or ours? We were planted here before the Prophet Abraham came, but it looks like they [Israelis] don't understand history or geography." Under the Oslo Accords, Israel agreed to deposit VAT tax receipts from goods purchased by Palestinians into the Palestinian treasury, which until 2000 were transferred directly to Arafat's personal accounts at Bank Leumi in Tel Aviv. In August 2002, the Israeli Military Intelligence Chief alleged Arafat's personal wealth was approximately $1.3 billion. In 2003, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) audited the PNA and found that Arafat had diverted $900 million in public funds to a special bank account controlled by himself and the PNA Chief Economic Financial adviser.

It had been decided, in principle, to remove Arafat from the Israeli-controlled West Bank. In an interview with Al Jazeera, Arafat responded to Ariel Sharon's suggestion that he be exiled permanently by stating, "Is it his [Sharon's] homeland or ours? We were planted here before the Prophet Abraham came, but it looks like they [Israelis] don't understand history or geography." Under the Oslo Peace Accords, Israel agreed to deposit VAT tax receipts from goods purchased by Palestinians into the Palestinian treasury, which until 2000 were transferred directly to Arafat's personal accounts at Bank Leumi in Tel Aviv. In August 2002, the Israeli Military Intelligence Chief claimed Arafat's personal wealth was approximately US$1.3 billion. In 2003, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) audited the PNA and found that Arafat had diverted $900 million in public funds to a special bank account controlled by himself and the PNA Chief Economic Financial Adviser, though the IMF did not allege improprieties and stated most of the funds were used to invest in Palestinian assets both domestically and abroad. A team of American accountants, hired by Arafat's own finance ministry, concluded in 2003 that part of his wealth was in a secret portfolio valued near $1 billion, including investments in a Coca-Cola bottling plant in Ramallah, a Tunisian cell phone company, and venture capital funds in the U.S. and the Cayman Islands. The head of the investigation stated that although the money originated from public funds like Palestinian taxes, virtually none was used for the Palestinian people; it was entirely controlled by Arafat, and none of these transactions were made public. A General Accounting Office investigation reported that Arafat and the PLO held over $10 billion in assets even when Arafat publicly claimed bankruptcy. Despite living a modest lifestyle, Dennis Ross, former Middle East negotiator for Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton, noted that Arafat's "walking-around money" supported a vast patronage system known as neopatrimonialism. Salam Fayyad, a former World Bank official and Arafat's appointed Finance Minister in 2002, stated that Arafat's commodity monopolies amounted to gouging his own people, especially in Gaza, which is poorer, calling it totally unacceptable and immoral, and claimed Arafat used $20 million from public funds to pay the leadership of the PNA security forces, the Preventive Security Service. Fuad Shubaki, Arafat's former financial aide, told the Israeli security service Shin Bet that Arafat used millions of dollars in aid money to buy weapons and support militant groups. During Israel's Operation Defensive Shield, Israeli forces recovered counterfeit money and documents from Arafat's Ramallah headquarters, showing that in 2001 he personally approved payments to Tanzim militants; the Palestinians claimed the counterfeit money was seized from criminal elements. The Israeli government attempted to assassinate Arafat for decades, including efforts to intercept and shoot down private aircraft and commercial airliners on which he was believed to be traveling. The assassination was initially assigned to Caesarea, the Mossad unit responsible for targeted killings, with shooting down a commercial airliner in international airspace over deep water considered preferable to make wreckage recovery and investigation difficult. Following Israel's 1982 invasion of Lebanon, Israeli Defense Minister Ariel Sharon established a special task force called "Salt Fish," headed by Meir Dagan and Rafi Eitan, to track Arafat's movements in Lebanon with the goal of killing him, as Sharon viewed Arafat as a "Jew murderer" and an important symbol in the war against terrorism. The Salt Fish task force bombed buildings where Arafat and senior PLO leaders were believed to be staying. Later renamed "Operation Goldfish," Israeli operatives followed Israeli journalist Uri Avnery to a meeting with Arafat in an unsuccessful attempt to kill him. In 2001, as prime minister, Sharon is believed to have committed to ending attempts to assassinate Arafat, though in April 2004, after the successful assassination of Hamas founder Sheikh Ahmed Yassin, Sharon stated that this commitment no longer existed. The first reports of Arafat's deteriorating health, attributed to influenza by his doctors, came on 25 October 2004, after he vomited during a staff meeting; his condition worsened over the following days. After visits by doctors from Tunisia, Jordan, and Egypt, and with Israel's agreement to allow travel, Arafat was flown from Ramallah to Jordan by a Jordanian military helicopter and then to France on a French military plane, where he was admitted to the Percy military hospital in Clamart, a suburb of Paris. On 3 November, he lapsed into a gradually deepening coma. Arafat was pronounced dead at 03:30 UTC on 11 November 2004 at the age of 75 from what French doctors called a massive hemorrhagic cerebrovascular accident (hemorrhagic stroke). Senior Palestinian officials initially withheld his medical records, and Arafat's wife refused an autopsy, citing Muslim practices. French doctors also noted that Arafat suffered from disseminated intravascular coagulation, though it is inconclusive what caused it. Upon his death, the Palestinian people entered a state of mourning, with Qur'anic prayers broadcast from mosque loudspeakers across the West Bank and Gaza Strip and tires burned in the streets. The Palestinian Authority and refugee camps in Lebanon declared 40 days of mourning. On 11 November 2004, a French Army guard of honour held a brief ceremony for Arafat, with his coffin draped in a Palestinian flag; a military band played the French and Palestinian national anthems and a Chopin funeral march. French President Jacques Chirac stood beside Arafat's coffin for about ten minutes, praising him as "a man of courage." The next day, Arafat's body was flown from Paris to Cairo by a French Air Force transport plane for a brief military funeral attended by several heads of state, prime ministers, and foreign ministers. Egypt's top Muslim cleric Sayed Tantawi led mourning prayers before the funeral procession. Israel refused Arafat's request to be buried near Masjid Al-Aqsa or anywhere in Jerusalem, citing security concerns and fearing his burial would strengthen Palestinian claims to East Jerusalem. Following the Cairo procession, Arafat was "temporarily" buried within the Mukataa in Ramallah, with tens of thousands of Palestinians attending. Arafat was buried in a stone, not wooden, coffin, and Palestinian spokesman Saeb Erekat stated he would be reburied in East Jerusalem once a Palestinian state was established. After Sheikh Taissir Tamimi discovered Arafat was buried improperly and in a coffin not in accordance with Islamic law, he was reburied on the morning of 13 November at around 3:00 a.m. On 10 November 2007, prior to the third anniversary of his death, President Mahmoud Abbas unveiled a mausoleum near Arafat's tomb. Numerous theories have circulated about Arafat's death, including poisoning (possibly by polonium), AIDS-related illnesses, liver disease, or a platelet disorder. In September 2005, an Israeli AIDS expert claimed Arafat showed all symptoms of AIDS based on medical records, but others, including Patrice Mangin of the University of Lausanne and The New York Times, disputed this, stating it was highly unlikely AIDS caused his death. Arafat's personal doctor Ashraf al-Kurdi and aide Bassam Abu Sharif maintained he was poisoned, possibly by thallium. A senior Israeli physician concluded he died from food poisoning. Both Israeli and Palestinian officials denied poisoning claims, and Palestinian foreign minister Nabil Shaath ruled out poisoning after discussions with Arafat's French doctors. On 4 July 2012, Al Jazeera published findings from a nine-month investigation that refuted rumors Arafat died of cancer, cirrhosis, or AIDS, noting he was in good health until falling ill on 12 October 2004, but revealed Swiss experts found traces of polonium in quantities far exceeding natural levels on Arafat's personal belongings. On 12 October 2013, The Lancet published a peer-reviewed article by Swiss experts analyzing 38 samples of Arafat's clothes and belongings and 37 polonium-free reference samples, suggesting polonium poisoning was possible. On 27 November 2012, three independent international teams—French, Swiss, and Russian—collected samples from Arafat's body and the surrounding soil in the Ramallah mausoleum. On 6 November 2013, Al Jazeera reported that the Swiss forensic team found polonium levels in Arafat's ribs and pelvis 18 to 36 times the average, though the amount had diminished by a factor of 2 million. François Bochud, head of the Swiss team, said the poisoning hypothesis by polonium was "reasonably supported," while forensic scientist Dave Barclay, retained by Al Jazeera, stated it was "absolutely certain" that polonium poisoning caused his illness, calling it "the smoking gun" given with malice. Derek Hill, a professor at University College London not involved in the investigation, said the evidence was strong but not overwhelming, noting a risk of contamination and that the findings represented a cautious interpretation of strong data. On 26 December 2013, a Russian scientific team released a report finding no trace of radioactive poisoning, after the French report detected polonium; Vladimir Uiba, head of the Federal Medical and Biological Agency, concluded Arafat died of natural causes and stated no further tests would be conducted. Unlike the Swiss report, the French and Russian reports were not made public at the time. The Swiss experts reviewed the French and Russian reports and argued that the radiologic data supported their conclusion of probable polonium poisoning. In March 2015, a French prosecutor closed a 2012 French inquiry, stating French experts believed the polonium and lead traces were environmental in nature. Palestinian official Wasel Abu Yousef criticized the 2013 report, calling it "politicized" and contrary to evidence that Arafat was killed by poisoning, and claimed it was an attempt to cover up what happened at Percy hospital.
